claim: Heat-killed E. coli (HK-E. coli) is a low-quality food that triggers cellular UPRER and immune response in C. elegans.
source: Here, we established a low-quality food evaluation assay system and found that heat-killed E. coli (HK-E. coli), a low-sugar food, triggers cellular UPRER and immune response.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F-G and throughout the manuscript.

claim: The physiological system for evaluating low-quality food depends on the UPRER (IRE-1/XBP-1) - Innate immunity (PMK-1/p38 MAPK) axis.
source: The physiological system for evaluating low-quality food depends on the UPRER (IRE-1/XBP-1) - Innate immunity (PMK-1/p38 MAPK) axis, particularly its neuronal function, which subsequently regulates feeding behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 5 showing the role of these pathways in food evaluation.

claim: Animals can adapt to a low-quality food environment through sugar supplementation, which inhibits the UPRER-PMK-1 regulated stress response by increasing vitamin C biosynthesis.
source: Moreover, animals can adapt to a low-quality food environment through sugar supplementation, which inhibits the UPRER -PMK-1 regulated stress response by increasing vitamin C biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4 showing the effects of sugar and vitamin C supplementation.

claim: Wild-type animals avoid HK-E. coli OP50 (HK-OP50) food in avoidance assays.
source: In the avoidance assay, wild-type animals avoided the HK-E. coli OP50 (HK-OP50) food (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Worms initially show no preference between live and heat-killed E. coli (1-2 hr), but eventually exhibit a preference for high-quality food (Live E. coli) up until the 17 hr mark.
source: Interestingly, in the food choice assay, animals initially showed no preference between the two types of food (1–2 hr), but eventually exhibited a preference for high-quality food (Live E. coli) up until the 17 hr mark (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This temporal pattern of food preference is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Worms depart from HK-E. coli after recognizing it as low-quality food source through ingestion.
source: This suggests that worms depart from the HK-E. coli after recognizing it as low-quality food source through ingestion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal food choice data showing delayed preference development.

claim: Stress response genes, including those related to biotic stimulus, immune response and response to stress, are up-regulated in animals fed with HK-E. coli OP50.
source: Gene-expression profiling revealed that stress response genes, including those related to biotic stimulus, immune response and response to stress, are up-regulated in animals fed with HK-E. coli OP50 (HK-OP50; Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 2a.

claim: 11 out of 62 UPRER target genes are up-regulated in animals fed with HK-E. coli.
source: Among these up-regulated genes, we identified 11 out of 62 of UPRER target genes (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: This specific quantification is stated in the text and supported by the Venn diagram in Figure 1D.

claim: About 50-80% of up-regulated genes in animals fed HK-E. coli overlap with genes responding to pathogenic bacteria.
source: Additionally, about 50–80% of up-regulated genes overlap with genes responding pathogenic bacteria (Nakad et al., 2016; Sinha et al., 2012; Figure 1E, Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to published data and supported by the Venn diagram in Figure 1E.

claim: The UPRER reporter (Phsp-4::GFP) is strongly induced in intestine and neurons by feeding HK-E. coli OP50.
source: Consistent with the results of the RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis, the UPRER reporter (Phsp-4::GFP) (Calfon et al., 2002) and immunity reporter (Pirg-5::GFP)(Bolz et al., 2010) were strongly induced in intestine (Figure 1F–G) and neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) by feeding unfavorable food (HK-E. coli OP50), suggesting that UPRER and immune pathways may respond to low-quality food (HK-E. coli OP50).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and supported by fluorescence images in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The immunity reporter (Pirg-5::GFP) is strongly induced in intestine and neurons by feeding HK-E. coli OP50.
source: Consistent with the results of the RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis, the UPRER reporter (Phsp-4::GFP) (Calfon et al., 2002) and immunity reporter (Pirg-5::GFP)(Bolz et al., 2010) were strongly induced in intestine (Figure 1F–G) and neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) by feeding unfavorable food (HK-E. coli OP50), suggesting that UPRER and immune pathways may respond to low-quality food (HK-E. coli OP50).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and supported by fluorescence images in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: UPRMt reporter (Phsp-6::GFP) is weakly induced under HK-E. coli feeding condition.
source: Moreover, UPRMt reporter (Phsp-6::GFP) (Yoneda et al., 2004) was weakly induced under HK-E. coli feeding condition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and starved worm did not induce UPRER and immunity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and supported by fluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Starved worms do not induce UPRER and immunity.
source: Moreover, UPRMt reporter (Phsp-6::GFP) (Yoneda et al., 2004) was weakly induced under HK-E. coli feeding condition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and starved worm did not induce UPRER and immunity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Low-quality food (HK-E. coli OP50) triggers a stress response pathway in animals, including UPRER and innate immune pathway.
source: Together, these findings suggest that low-quality food (HK-E. coli OP50) triggers a stress response pathway in animals, including UPRER and innate immune pathway.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Activation of the UPRER by HK-E. coli depends on the IRE-1/XBP-1 branch.
source: We observed no difference in Phsp-4::GFP induction with atf-4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) or atf-6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) RNAi-mediated knockdown in animals fed with HK-E. coli. However, knockdown of ire-1/xbp-1 or mutation of xbp-1 reduced GFP fluorescence (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by experimental data in Figures 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: 64% of the 11 differentially expressed UPRER target genes in animals fed with HK-E. coli are IRE-mediated genes.
source: Among the 11 differentially expressed UPRER target genes in animals fed with HK-E. coli from RNA-seq (Figure 1D), 64% of the genes are IRE-mediated genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, Supplementary file 2d).
evidence: This specific percentage is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The mRNA level of IRE-1-mediated splicing of xbp-1 is induced in animals fed with HK-E. coli OP50.
source: The mRNA level of IRE-1-mediated splicing of xbp-1 (Calfon et al., 2002) is also induced in animals fed with HK-E. coli OP50 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and supported by qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: xbp-1 mutants have a significantly decreased likelihood of leaving HK-E. coli.
source: The results show that xbp-1 mutants had a significantly decreased likelihood of leaving of HK-E. coli, which was rescued by expressing xbp-1 in neuron rather than intestine (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by behavioral assay data in Figure 2C.

claim: XBP-1-dependent UPRER activation in neurons is critical for animals to specifically evaluate low-quality food (HK-E. coli).
source: This indicates that XBP-1-dependent UPRER activation in neuron is critical for animals to specific evaluate low-quality food (HK-E. coli).
evidence: This is an inference based on the tissue-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 82 out of 409 PMK-1-dependent genes are up-regulated in animals fed with HK-E. coli.
source: Among these up-regulated genes, 82 out of 409 of PMK-1-dependent genes (Fletcher et al., 2019) were identified (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This specific quantification is stated in the text with citation and supported by the Venn diagram in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The induction of Pirg-5::GFP is abolished in pmk-1 knockdown animals fed with HK-E. coli.
source: Moreover, the induction of Pirg-5::GFP was abolished in pmk-1 knockdown animals fed with HK-E. coli (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence data in Figure 2D.

claim: The phosphorylated PMK-1 (p-PMK-1) level is prominently increased in wild-type N2 animals fed HK-E. coli compared to feeding E. coli OP50.
source: Third, we found that the phosphorylated PMK-1 (p-PMK-1) level was prominently increased in wild-type N2 animals fed HK-E. coli compared to feeding E. coli OP50 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 2E.

claim: pmk-1 mutants have a decreased likelihood of leaving HK-E. coli, which is rescued by expressing pmk-1 in neurons rather than intestine.
source: Finally, pmk-1 mutants had a decreased likelihood of leaving of HK-E. coli, which was rescued by expressing pmk-1 in neurons rather than intestine (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by behavioral assay data in Figure 2F.

claim: PMK-1 regulated immune pathway evaluates low-quality food, especially the neuronal PMK-1 has a critical function for food quality response.
source: These data suggest that PMK-1 regulated immune pathway evaluates low-quality food, especially the neuronal PMK-1 has a critical function for food quality response.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data showing tissue-specific rescue in Figure 2F.

claim: Pirg-5::GFP induction and PMK-1 activation are decreased in animals with xbp-1 mutation or knockdown when fed with HK-E. coli.
source: We found that Pirg-5::GFP induction (Figure 2—figure supplements 1I and 2A) and PMK-1 activation (Figure 2E) were decreased in animals with xbp-1 mutation or knockdown when fed with HK-E. coli, suggesting that XBP-1 could regulate PMK-1 under this condition.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplements 1I and 2A.

claim: XBP-1-dependent UPRER activation is not regulated by PMK-1.
source: Additionally, Phsp-4::GFP induction under HK-E. coli was not affected in animals with pmk-1 RNAi (Figure 2—figure supplements 1D and 2B), indicating that XBP-1-dependent UPRER activation is not regulated by PMK-1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplements 1D and 2B.

claim: PMK-1 is downstream of XBP-1 in responding to low-quality food.
source: Finally, we constructed a double mutant of xbp-1 and pmk-1 and found that the food avoidance phenotype of the double mutant was similar to the pmk-1 mutant (Figure 2G), indicating that PMK-1 is downstream of XBP-1 in responding to low-quality food.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by genetic epistasis data in Figure 2G.

claim: N2 and xbp-1 mutant worms can escape from inedible food (Saprophytic staphylococci), whereas pmk-1 mutant worms do not exhibit this avoidance behavior.
source: However, both N2 and xbp-1 mutant worms were able to escape from inedible food (N2 was predominantly found on the border areas of the bacterial lawn and xbp-1 mutant worms on border and in), Saprophytic staphylococci, whereas pmk-1 mutant worms did not exhibit this avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by behavioral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: N2 and xbp-1 mutant worms exhibit pronounced avoidance behavior when exposed to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, whereas pmk-1 mutant worms are more susceptible to infection.
source: Notably, N2 and xbp-1 mutant worms exhibited even more pronounced avoidance behavior when exposed to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, whereas pmk-1 mutant worms were more susceptible to infection by this pathogen (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by behavioral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The UPR-Immunity pathway plays a crucial role in helping animals avoid low-quality food (HK-E. coli) by triggering an avoidance response.
source: These findings suggest that the UPR-Immunity pathway plays a crucial role in helping animals avoid low-quality food (HK-E. coli) by triggering an avoidance response.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data comparing responses to different food types.

claim: The Innate immunity pathway mediated by PMK-1/p38 MAPK plays a key role in evaluating unfavorable food sources including HK-E. coli, Saprophytic staphylococci, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: In contrast, the Innate immunity pathway, which is mediated by PMK-1/p38 MAPK, appears to play a key role in evaluating unfavorable food sources, such as HK-E. coli, Saprophytic staphylococci, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and helping animals avoid these environments.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data comparing responses to different food types in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Animals fed HK-yfbR have a decreased ability to leave food compared to HK-K12.
source: Animals fed HK-yfbR, which catalyzes carbohydrate derivative metabolic process (Weiss, 2007), had a decreased ability to leave food (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 3a), indicating that HK-yfbR may be a higher quality food for animals compared to HK-K12.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and supported by behavioral data in Figure 3A.

claim: HK-yfbR may be a higher quality food for animals compared to HK-K12.
source: Animals fed HK-yfbR, which catalyzes carbohydrate derivative metabolic process (Weiss, 2007), had a decreased ability to leave food (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 3a), indicating that HK-yfbR may be a higher quality food for animals compared to HK-K12.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data showing reduced avoidance of HK-yfbR.

claim: The level of 13 metabolites are similar between HK-yfbR and Live-K12, but significantly changed in HK-K12.
source: We found that the level of 13 metabolites were similar between HK-yfbR and Live-K12, but significantly changed in HK-K12 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, and Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Genes involved in glycolysis/gluconeogenesis are up-regulated in animals fed with HK-E. coli.
source: We also found that genes involved in glycolysis/gluconeogenesis were up-regulated in animals fed with HK-E. coli (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that glycolysis/gluconeogenesis metabolism is disordered in animals fed with HK-E. coli, which may result from changes in sugar/carbohydrate intake.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by KEGG enrichment analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Carbohydrates (D-trehalose, lactose, and D-(+)-sucrose) are decreased in HK-E. coli.
source: The carbohydrates (D-trehalose, lactose, and D-(+)-sucrose) were also decreased in HK-E. coli (Figure 3B), suggesting that carbohydrate deficiency may induce stress response and avoidance behavior in animals feeding HK-E. coli.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3B.

claim: Lactose and D-(+)-sucrose supplementation inhibit HK-E. coli induced UPRER.
source: Thirdly, to determine which carbohydrate inhibits stress response in animals, we supplemented each metabolite to HK-E. coli and found that only Lactose, and D-(+)-sucrose inhibited HK-E. coli induced UPRER (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence data in Figures 3C-D.

claim: D-(+)-glucose supplementation inhibits HK-E. coli induced UPRER, immune response, and avoidance.
source: We found that D-(+)-glucose supplementation also inhibited HK-E. coli induced UPRER (Figure 3E), immune response (Figure 3F and G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D) and avoidance (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by multiple experimental data in Figures 3E-H.

claim: Sugar supplementation does not affect UPRER and immunity in normal food (OP50) or starved condition (NGM).
source: Moreover, sugar supplementation did not affect UPRER and immunity in normal food (OP50) or starved condition (NGM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: Supplementing HK-E. coli with carbohydrates (D-Glc, D-GlcA) does not support animal development.
source: To our surprise, supplementing HK-E. coli with carbohydrates (D-Glc, D-GlcA) did not support animal development (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G), suggesting that carbohydrates are not sufficient for supporting animal growth on this food source.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by developmental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Carbohydrates are critical for inhibiting the UPRER-immune response induced by sugar deficiency in HK-E. coli.
source: However, we did find that carbohydrates are critical for inhibiting the UPRER-immune response induced by sugar deficiency in HK-E. coli.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data showing sugar supplementation effects.

claim: The vitamin C level increases in C. elegans when fed with HK-yfbR, a high-carbohydrate food compared to HK-E. coli.
source: Firstly, we observed an increase in the vitamin C level in C. elegans when fed with HK-yfbR (Figure 4B), a high-carbohydrate food compared to HK-E. coli (Figure 3B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by vitamin C measurement data in Figure 4B.

claim: The VC level increases when D-glucose or D-glucuronate (D-GlcA) is added to HK-E. coli.
source: The VC level also increased when D-glucose (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) or D-glucuronate (D-GlcA) was added to HK-E. coli (Figure 4C), which was abolished by knocking down VC biosynthesis genes (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by vitamin C measurement data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Addition of sugar supplementation promotes VC synthesis in animals fed with HK-E. coli.
source: This suggests that addition of sugar supplementation promotes VC synthesis in animals fed with HK-E. coli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the vitamin C measurement data showing increased levels with sugar supplementation.

claim: VC or D-glucuronate (D-GlcA) supplementation inhibits HK-E. coli induced UPRER, immune response, and food avoidance.
source: We found that VC or D-glucuronate (D-GlcA) supplementation inhibits HK-E. coli induced UPRER (Figure 4D), immune response including irg-5/sysm-1 reporter expression (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and p-PMK-1 (Figure 4F and G), as well as food avoidance (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by multiple experimental data in Figures 4D-H.

claim: Suppression of HK-E. coli induced UPRER, immune response and food avoidance by D-GlcA/sugar supplementation is abolished in animals with RNAi of VC biosynthesis genes.
source: We found that suppression of HK-E. coli induced UPRER (Figure 4I), immune response (Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and food avoidance (Figure 4K) by D-GlcA/sugar supplementation was abolished in animals with RNAi of VC biosynthesis genes.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by experimental data in Figures 4I-K.

claim: VC supplementation suppresses UPRER, immune response and food avoidance in animals with or without RNAi of VC biosynthesis genes.
source: However, VC supplementation still suppressed the UPRER (Figure 4I), immune response (Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and food avoidance (Figure 4K), and increased the food preference (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) in animals with or without RNAi of VC biosynthesis genes.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by experimental data in Figures 4I-K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: VC, as the final metabolite synthesized from D-glucose, is critical for evaluating low-quality food response in animals.
source: This suggests that VC, as the final metabolite synthesized from D-glucose, is critical for evaluating low-quality food response in animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic and supplementation experiments showing the role of VC biosynthesis.

claim: The vitamin C biosynthesis pathway is critical for evaluating whether food is of higher quality and can be eaten by animals.
source: Together, these data indicate that the vitamin C biosynthesis pathway is critical for evaluating whether food is of higher quality and can be eaten by animals.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data showing the role of vitamin C biosynthesis in food evaluation.

claim: Animals can improve their VC levels to adapt to bad food environment.
source: It also suggests that animals could improve their VC levels to adapt to bad food environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing increased VC synthesis with sugar supplementation in low-quality food conditions.

claim: D-Glc, D-GlcA, or VC supplementation increases the preference for heat-killed bacteria, which is suppressed in xbp-1 or pmk-1 mutant animals.
source: Interestingly, D-Glc and D-GlcA (Figure 5B and C) or VC (Figure 5D) supplementation increased the preference for heat-killed bacteria, which was suppressed in xbp-1 or pmk-1 mutant animals.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by food selection assay data in Figures 5B-D.

claim: Neuronal XBP-1 and PMK-1 are critical for physiological food elevation system for monitoring the level of sugar and VC under low-quality food condition.
source: However, this preference was also rescued in xbp-1 or pmk-1 mutant animals by expressing XBP-1 or PMK-1 in neurons rather than intestine (Figure 5B–D), indicating that neuronal XBP-1 and PMK-1 are critical for physiological food elevation system for monitoring the level of sugar and VC under low-quality food condition.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by tissue-specific rescue data in Figures 5B-D.

claim: Heat-killed E. coli (HK-E. coli) is a low-quality food source that cannot support the growth of C. elegans larvae.
source: Previous studies have shown that heat-killed E. coli (HK-E. coli) is a low-quality food source that cannot support the growth of C. elegans larvae (Qi and Han, 2018; Qi et al., 2017), whereas supplementation with vitamin B2 (VB2) can restore animal growth (Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to previous studies.

claim: Supplementation with vitamin B2 (VB2) can restore animal growth on HK-E. coli.
source: Previous studies have shown that heat-killed E. coli (HK-E. coli) is a low-quality food source that cannot support the growth of C. elegans larvae (Qi and Han, 2018; Qi et al., 2017), whereas supplementation with vitamin B2 (VB2) can restore animal growth (Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to a previous study.

claim: Animals maintain similar VC levels when fed ideal food (live E. coli) compared to low-quality food (HK-E. coli).
source: However, our results show that animals maintain similar VC levels when fed ideal food (live E. coli) compared to low-quality food (HK-E. coli; Figure 4B), suggesting that animals do not stimulate VC biosynthesis under favorable food conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by vitamin C measurement data in Figure 4B.

claim: Animals do not stimulate VC biosynthesis under favorable food conditions.
source: However, our results show that animals maintain similar VC levels when fed ideal food (live E. coli) compared to low-quality food (HK-E. coli; Figure 4B), suggesting that animals do not stimulate VC biosynthesis under favorable food conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the vitamin C measurement data showing similar levels in different food conditions.

claim: Glucose boosts the animal's ability to adapt to unfavorable food environments by increasing VC levels, but not in favorable food conditions.
source: These data indicate that glucose boosts the animal's ability to adapt to unfavorable food environments by increasing VC levels, but not in favorable food conditions.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data showing differential effects of glucose supplementation in different food conditions.

claim: The TORC1-ELT-2 pathway acts as master regulators in intestine that evaluate vitamin B2 deficiency in low-quality food (HK-E. coli) and regulate gut digestive activity to impact animal's food behavior.
source: In our previous study, we discovered that the TORC1-ELT-2 pathway, acting as master regulators in intestine, evaluates vitamin B2 deficiency in low-quality food (HK-E. coli) and regulates gut digestive activity to impact animal's food behavior (Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The Unfolded Protein Response (UPRER) is activated by various stresses, including infection and nutrition deficiency, which disrupt the homeostasis of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: One of the cellular stress response pathways, the Unfolded Protein Response (UPRER), is activated by various stresses, including infection and nutrition deficiency, which disrupt the homeostasis of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Hetz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to established knowledge.

claim: The activation of UPRER, specifically in the nervous system, promotes changes in feeding and foraging behavior.
source: The activation of UPRER, specifically in the nervous system, has been shown to promote changes in feeding and foraging behavior (Özbey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to published research.

claim: The p38 PMK-1 pathway is crucial for regulating the expression of secreted innate immune effectors and is essential for survival during infection.
source: The p38 PMK-1 pathway is also crucial for regulating the expression of secreted innate immune effectors and is essential for survival during infection (Troemel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to published research.

claim: Inhibition of ER function promotes C. elegans avoidance of toxic food, which employs the MLK-1/MEK-1/KGB-1 pathway.
source: Previously finding have shown that inhibition of ER function promotes C. elegans avoid to the toxic food, which employs the MLK-1/MEK-1/KGB-1 pathway (Melo and Ruvkun, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to published research.

claim: HK-E. coli induced avoidance behavior is independent of the KGB-1 pathway.
source: Notably, HK-E. coli induced avoidance behavior is independent of the KGB-1 pathway (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: XBP1 deficiency in intestinal epithelial cells leads to IRE1a hyperactivation and increased JNK phosphorylation in the epithelial compartment in vivo.
source: Previous studies have shown that XBP1 deficiency in intestinal epithelial cells leads to IRE1a hyperactivation and increased JNK phosphorylation in the epithelial compartment in vivo (Kaser et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to published research.

claim: The IRE1-XBP1 axis is a critical protective branch of the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) induced secondary to an innate immune response in the presence of P. aeruginosa.
source: The IRE1-XBP1 axis has been identified as a critical protective branch of the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) induced secondary to an innate immune response in the presence of P. aeruginosa (Kaser and Blumberg, 2010; Richardson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to published research.

claim: The p38 MAPK directly acts on the phosphorylation of IRE-1 to promote the stress response.
source: The p38 MAPK has also been shown to directly act on the phosphorylation of IRE-1 to promote the stress response (Guan et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to published research.

claim: IRE-1 confers cold resistance independently of XBP-1 by activating JNK-1 MAPK.
source: Interestingly, IRE-1 has been found to confer cold resistance independently of XBP-1 by activating JNK-1 MAPK (Melo and Ruvkun, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to published research.

claim: The UPRER (IRE-1/XBP-1) positively regulates Innate Immunity (PMK-1/p38 MAPK) under HK-E. coli food conditions.
source: In contrast, our study reveals a new mechanism where the UPRER (IRE-1/XBP-1) positively regulates Innate Immunity (PMK-1/p38 MAPK) under HK-E. coli food conditions, establishing a novel physiological food evaluation system that activates the cellular stress response program.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Activating innate immunity (PMK-1 MAPK) leads to a reduction in translation.
source: A previous study has shown that activating innate immunity (PMK-1 MAPK) leads to a reduction in translation (Weaver et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to published research.

claim: PMK-1 activation causes a shutdown of food digestion in animals.
source: Our own previous research has also demonstrated that PMK-1 activation causes a shutdown of food digestion in animals (Geng et al., 2022), likely to reduce protein translation and cellular metabolism.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to the authors' previous research.

claim: Total translation ability is significantly reduced in animals fed with HK-E. coli.
source: To investigate this further, we measured the translation level of animals fed with HK-E. coli and found that total translation ability is significantly reduced in these animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Activating innate immunity (PMK-1 MAPK) may serve as a mechanism to slow down translation progress, thereby alleviating the pressure on the unfolded protein response (UPR) and preventing excessive UPRER activation.
source: This finding suggests that activating innate immunity (PMK-1 MAPK) may serve as a mechanism to slow down translation progress, thereby alleviating the pressure on the unfolded protein response (UPR) and preventing excessive UPRER activation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the translation data and known functions of PMK-1.

claim: Vitamin C is an important physiological antioxidant and a cofactor for a family of biosynthetic and gene regulatory monooxygenase and dioxygenase enzymes.
source: Vitamin C is an important physiological antioxidant and a cofactor for a family of biosynthetic and gene regulatory monooxygenase and dioxygenase enzymes. It is also required for the biosynthesis of collagen, L-carnitine, and certain neurotransmitters (Carr and Frei, 1999; Li and Schellhorn, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to established knowledge.

claim: Vitamin C is required for the biosynthesis of collagen, L-carnitine, and certain neurotransmitters.
source: Vitamin C is an important physiological antioxidant and a cofactor for a family of biosynthetic and gene regulatory monooxygenase and dioxygenase enzymes. It is also required for the biosynthesis of collagen, L-carnitine, and certain neurotransmitters (Carr and Frei, 1999; Li and Schellhorn, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to established knowledge.

claim: VC helps animals to protect neurons, defend against excessive immune response, and inhibit inflammatory and ER stress.
